mcqs.question: Which of the following best defines electron gain enthalpy?

options.A: Energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom
options.B: Energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom
options.C: Energy change when an atom forms a cation
options.D: Energy change when an atom forms a covalent bond

mcqs.answer: Energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom
mcqs.explanation: Electron gain enthalpy (ΔEg) is the energy change that occurs when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron. It is usually negative because energy is released. Option B describes ionisation enthalpy, C and D are unrelated processes.

mcqs.question: Across a period from left to right, the electron gain enthalpy generally becomes:
mcqs.explanation: Moving across a period, atomic size decreases and nuclear attraction increases, so adding an electron releases more energy, making the electron gain enthalpy more negative. The other options contradict this observed trend.

mcqs.question: Which element shows a more negative electron gain enthalpy, indicating a greater tendency to gain an electron?

options.C: Both have the same electron gain enthalpy
options.D: Neither; both have positive electron gain enthalpy

mcqs.explanation: Chlorine, a halogen, has a highly negative electron gain enthalpy because it readily accepts an electron to achieve a noble‑gas configuration. Sodium, a metal, has a much less negative (often positive) value. Hence option B is correct.

mcqs.question: Nitrogen (Z = 7) has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than oxygen, even though it lies to the left of oxygen in the same period. Which reason best explains this exception?

options.A: Nitrogen has a half‑filled 2p subshell, which is relatively stable
options.B: Nitrogen possesses a larger nuclear charge than oxygen
options.C: Nitrogen atoms are larger, reducing electron‑nucleus attraction
options.D: Oxygen is more electronegative, making its electron gain enthalpy less negative

mcqs.answer: Nitrogen has a half‑filled 2p subshell, which is relatively stable
mcqs.explanation: The half‑filled 2p³ configuration of nitrogen provides extra stability, so adding an electron disrupts this stability and requires energy, resulting in a less negative (or even positive) electron gain enthalpy. Options B and C are inaccurate, and D reverses the trend.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about electron gain enthalpy is incorrect?

options.A: It is the energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom
options.B: It is always a positive quantity
options.C: It is denoted by the symbol ΔEg
options.D: Its magnitude can be compared across elements to assess their tendency to gain electrons

mcqs.answer: It is always a positive quantity
mcqs.explanation: Electron gain enthalpy is often negative because energy is released when an electron is added. Some elements (e.g., Be, N) have positive values, but it is not universally positive. Hence statement B is the misconception.

mcqs.question: Why does electron gain enthalpy become more negative when moving from left to right across a period?

options.A: Atomic radius decreases, increasing the attraction between the nucleus and the added electron
options.B: Shielding effect increases, reducing effective nuclear charge
options.C: Nuclear charge decreases across the period
options.D: Electron‑electron repulsion in the outer shell increases dramatically

mcqs.answer: Atomic radius decreases, increasing the attraction between the nucleus and the added electron
mcqs.explanation: Across a period, added protons increase nuclear charge while the shielding remains almost constant, causing the atomic radius to shrink. The stronger nucleus‑electron attraction makes the addition of an electron release more energy (more negative ΔEg). Options B, C, and D describe opposite or unrelated effects.

mcqs.question: Arrange the following elements in order of decreasing (more negative to less negative) electron gain enthalpy:
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen generally has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine because fluorine’s small size leads to increased electron‑electron repulsion. Nitrogen’s half‑filled p subshell makes its value less negative, and carbon is even less negative. Therefore the correct decreasing order is O > F > N > C. The other options misplace the relative magnitudes.

mcqs.question: Why is the electron gain enthalpy of beryllium (Be) positive (i.e., energy is absorbed) when an electron is added to a gaseous Be atom?

options.A: Adding an electron would start filling the higher‑energy 2p orbital after the stable 2s² configuration
options.B: Be has an exceptionally high nuclear charge that repels incoming electrons
options.C: Be possesses a very large atomic radius, weakening nuclear attraction
options.D: Be has a half‑filled d subshell that stabilises the atom

mcqs.answer: Adding an electron would start filling the higher‑energy 2p orbital after the stable 2s² configuration
mcqs.explanation: Be’s electron configuration is 1s² 2s². The next electron must enter the 2p subshell, which is higher in energy than the filled 2s subshell, so energy must be supplied, giving a positive electron gain enthalpy. Options B and C are incorrect because Be’s nuclear charge is modest and its radius is small. Option D is irrelevant as Be has no d electrons.
